turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Got his vitals while he was checking in. Blood pressure 142 over 88... no, 86. Pulse 92.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Oxygen?
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): 93 percent on room air, respirations 22. Spirometry you ordered, FEV1 one point six... sorry, one point nine liters, 62 percent predicted.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the FVC?
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): 3.2 liters, 81 percent. Ratio comes out to 0.59. He keeps saying he's fine.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bring him in.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Hey. Whole lot of fuss over a little cough.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Morning cough?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Just mornings. It clears. It's nothing.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Uh, a few...
[SEG0012] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, the pharmacy list just popped up, you want me to—
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not now.
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Three weeks. No, wait, two months. It started before that bug.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Only on the stairs. I'm out of shape, that's all. Not a real problem.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): The garage was a nightmare, I almost turned around and went home.
[SEG0019] person_1 (NURSE): He said the same thing at the desk.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever. Not now.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood when you cough?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Course not.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Wheezing?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bringing anything up?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): A little clear junk in the morning. Barely anything.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does it wake you at night?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Nah. I sleep fine. Neighbor's dog is worse, starts barking at five and—
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay on the cough. You smoke.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): About ten a day.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ten.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Well, maybe twenty. Depends. I've cut way back.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many years?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Forty years... no. I started at twenty-eight, I'm fifty-eight, so thirty years. Doesn't mean the cough is from that.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): You use inhalers?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): The blue one. Albuterol. Two puffs when I need it.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): How often?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Every day... no, more like twice a week. If that.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): A maintenance inhaler too?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Symbicort... wait, no, it's Advair. Purple diskus. The 100... no, 250/50.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Twice a day, as it was prescribed?
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is that a yes?
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really. I forget. It sits in the bathroom.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): You were treated for a chest infection.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): Urgent care made a big deal, like three weeks ago. I wasn't that sick.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): What antibiotic?
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): Amoxicillin, 500 milligrams, three times a day, for ten days... actually the bottle said seven. I finished every pill.
[SEG0049] person_1 (NURSE): Pharmacy shows Advair last filled four months ago, one diskus. Albuterol was filled last month.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the Advair has been sitting around.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): I use it. Sometimes. Don't give me that look.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Deep breaths. I'm listening.
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breath sounds diminished at both bases. Expiratory wheeze on the right. No crackles.
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): See? Not terrible.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me see your ankles.
[SEG0057] person_3 (PATIENT): They're fine. I walk all day at the yard, well, I used to, before they stuck me on dispatch—
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): No swelling.
[SEG0059] person_2 (DOCTOR): That ratio, 0.59, FEV1 at 62 percent, is an obstructive pattern.
[SEG0060] person_3 (PATIENT): Meaning what.
[SEG0061] person_2 (DOCTOR): Working impression is COPD from the smoking. Provisional. Lingering bronchitis from that infection isn't fully off the table.
[SEG0062] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't have COPD. It's a morning thing. People who smoke cough.
[SEG0063] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm ordering a chest x-ray.
[SEG0064] person_3 (PATIENT): For this?
[SEG0065] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. Today, if radiology can fit you.
[SEG0066] person_3 (PATIENT): Fine. Whatever.
[SEG0067] person_2 (DOCTOR): Advair, one inhalation twice a day, every day. Not when you happen to remember.
[SEG0068] person_3 (PATIENT): Sure, sure.
[SEG0069] person_2 (DOCTOR): Albuterol stays two puffs when you get winded. Don't wait until you can barely talk.
[SEG0070] person_3 (PATIENT): I already do that.
[SEG0071] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll refer you to the state quitline.
[SEG0072] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't need a class. I'm basically down to—
[SEG0073] person_2 (DOCTOR): And I'm sending a nicotine patch, 21 milligrams, one a day.
[SEG0074] person_3 (PATIENT): I won't wear it.
[SEG0075] person_2 (DOCTOR): The prescription will still be there. Use it if you actually want off the cigarettes.
[SEG0076] person_3 (PATIENT): Hmph. We'll see.
[SEG0077] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in six weeks. If you're breathing harder at rest, come in sooner.
[SEG0078] person_3 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Can I go? Meter's running out, I parked on Third.
[SEG0079] person_2 (DOCTOR): We're done. She'll get you to x-ray.
[SEG0080] person_1 (NURSE): I'll print the patch and walk you down. Also your truck keys were up front.
[SEG0081] person_3 (PATIENT): Right. Thanks. Told you it's not even that bad.

spec.situation: Long-term smoker with morning cough and breathlessness; minimises smoking ('about ten a day... maybe twenty'), inhalers used irregularly, a recent chest infection; spirometry numbers read aloud; quitting support offered.
features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

bad.reason: Spirometry was completed, but transcript does not say nurse performed it, only reported results.

omissions.text: Intermittent wheezing was reported by the patient ('Sometimes, not really').
Albuterol use frequency is inconsistently reported: patient first said 'Every day' then corrected to 'more like twice a week, if that.'
Advair adherence is poor/nonadherent: patient ultimately said he forgets it and uses it only sometimes; pharmacy also showed Advair last filled four months ago.
The patient recently had a chest infection treated at urgent care about three weeks ago.
Amoxicillin course duration is uncertain/conflicting: patient said 'for ten days... actually the bottle said seven' and finished every pill.
Doctor advised chest x-ray should be done today if radiology can fit him.
There is real disagreement/resistance about the COPD assessment: patient explicitly said 'I don't have COPD.'
There is real disagreement/resistance about smoking-cessation treatment: after nicotine patch was prescribed, patient said 'I won't wear it.'
